papers.title: The Metacomplexity Structure of Search Problems
papers.abstract: We study the metacomplexity tasks of refuting an algorithm for a given search problem or refuting a mapping reduction between two search problems. We show that these tasks are deeply related to the structure of the lattice of search problems under mapping reductions: the "refutation of a reduction" task amounts to a certain Heyting-type arrow in this lattice. We then give several structural complexity results about search problems and show they have implications for metacomplexity. First, by relating metacomplexity to a Heyting algebra structure, we are able to translate results from intuitionistic logic into complexity theoretic consequences. For example, the propositional logic identity $x\wedge \neg x=\bot$ translates to the following complexity-theoretic fact: if a search problem $R$ reduces to both $S$ and to the refutation task of $S$, then $R$ is in $\mathsf{FP}$. All such logical identities that hold in intuitionistic logic translate to complexity in a black box way. We find prime ideals of the reducibility lattice of search problems; as a consequence, we show that for any verifiable search problem $S$, either $S$ is in $(\mathsf{FP/poly})_{io}$ or else the refutation task of $S$ is in $(\mathsf{FP/poly})_{io}$. Similarly, either $S$ has infinitely-often heuristic algorithms or else the refutation task of $S$ has infinitely often heuristic algorithms. Finally, we give a structural result that may be of independent interest: any "tamely semantic" class of search problems (one which can be enumerated using a Halting oracle) is characterized by its decidably verifiable hard problems.

papers.title: Convexity is overrated: Shortest paths on 4-polytopes are hard to compute
papers.abstract: We prove that computing geodesic distance on the boundary of a rational convex $4$-polytope is NP-hard. We then construct rational $4$-polytopes with two rational points joined by exponentially many shortest paths of equal rational length, disproving several conjectures along the way. For the same problem, we also prove SQRTSUM-hardness under deterministic polynomial-time Turing reductions. By a separate argument, we show that the square of the geodesic distance between distinct rational boundary points of a rational convex polytope is a totally positive multiquadratic number.

papers.title: Fundamentals for Binary Classification Under Label Noise
papers.abstract: This chapter surveys fundamental results for binary classification under label noise. Binary classification under label noise involves training models on datasets where class labels are partially incorrect, leading to degraded performance and misclassification. We distinguish poisoning attacks from noise processes and formalize random classification noise, Massart noise, and malicious classification noise within the probably approximately correct (PAC) framework. These models capture different adversarial strengths and data-generation realities. We then highlight some core ideas and representative results. In particular, we explain why random classification noise preserves the expected ordering of hypotheses and thus supports learning using the empirical risk minimization (ERM) principle, how sample complexity depends on the noise rate, and why learning algorithms often require an upper bound on the corruption level, as well as how such a bound may be estimated from data in the case of random classification noise. We also discuss computational aspects of ERM under noise and present a canonical negative result technique -- the method of induced distributions -- within the malicious noise model where the adversary has more power and may affect not only the label of an example but also the instance. We conclude with pointers to related work and a taxonomy that organizes classical label-noise models using the NCAR/NAR/NNAR lens.

papers.title: Products of Distinguisher Hulls
papers.abstract: The distinguisher hull of two distributions is the convex hull of the pairs of acceptance probabilities of tests in a specified class. We study its behavior under independent products for size-bounded Boolean circuits. We derive a geometric consequence of Dwork and Tankala's supersimulator theorem (FOCS 2026), giving a substantially different proof of approximate product containment for distinguisher hulls. In particular, our construction uses nonadaptive sampling in place of adaptive score corrections.

papers.title: Deterministic Parameterized Inapproximability of the Shortest Vector and Minimum Distance Problems
papers.abstract: The Shortest Vector Problem (SVP) and the Minimum Distance Problem (MDP) are central computational problems on lattices and linear codes, respectively. For every computable real $p\ge1$ and any constant factor, we prove that the parameterized SVP in the $\ell_p$ norm, with the distance threshold as the parameter, is W[1]-hard to approximate within factor $\gamma$ under deterministic reductions. The same method shows that, for every finite field, the parameterized MDP is W[1]-hard to approximate within any constant factor under deterministic reductions.

papers.title: Degree Lower Bounds for Symmetric Boolean Functions: Breaking the Prime-Gap Barrier
papers.abstract: We prove that every nonconstant symmetric Boolean function on $n$ variables has exact real polynomial degree at least $n-O(n^{1/3}(\log n)^{2/3})$. This makes progress toward the conjecture of von zur Gathen and Roche that the degree is always at least $n-3$. The original prime-gap argument of von zur Gathen and Roche yields a degree deficit of $O(n^{0.525})$ using the theorem of Baker, Harman, and Pintz, or $O(n^{0.52})$ using an estimate claimed in a recent preprint. Our $\widetilde{O}(n^{1/3})$ bound on the degree deficit improves upon the $\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{n})$ bound obtainable from the prime-gap approach, even assuming the Riemann hypothesis or Legendre's conjecture. Notably, our proof avoids prime-gap estimates entirely. The proof combines vanishing binomial moments with the arithmetic of linear recurrences. A quantitative form of the integer Hankel determinant method in the P\'olya--Carlson theorem forces the function's values on a central interval of Hamming weights to satisfy a short rational recurrence. A second determinant argument bounds the number of characteristic roots near $-1$. Through the binomial transform, these roots can then be cancelled by a polynomial test of degree below the deficit. An integer annihilator and contour estimates make the test isolate the first failure of the recurrence, yielding a contradiction with the vanishing-moment conditions. If the recurrence agrees with the function on a sufficiently long interval, arithmetic height bounds instead force a bounded period, which is ruled out by a separate polynomial test. Every numbered result in the paper has been formally verified in Lean~4.

papers.title: The low-degree sample complexity of clustering Gaussian mixtures with more groups than dimensions
papers.abstract: We study the computational limits of clustering $n$ observations drawn from a mixture of $K$ isotropic Gaussian distributions in $\mathbb R^d$, when the number $K$ of groups is much larger than the dimension $d$. In this regime, distance-based and spectral procedures require a squared separation $\Delta^2$ of order $\sqrt d$. In contrast, tensor-based procedures cluster at a polylogarithmic separation but need a sample size that is a large polynomial of $dK$, and the low-degree lower bounds known for random centers only show that $n$ must exceed $dK^2$. Focusing on normally distributed centers, we characterize the minimal separation for clustering with low-degree polynomials in the regime $K>d$, through a low-degree lower bound and a matching upper bound, up to subpolynomial factors. In particular, for $K=d^{p/2}$ with $p> 2$ a real number, we show that a sample size of the order of $K^3 d^{(\lceil p\rceil-p)/2}$ is required to recover the clustering with subpolynomial separation, and that it suffices when $p$ is not an integer.

papers.title: The computational complexity of bosonic Lindbladian fixed points
papers.abstract: We study the computational complexity of estimating observables and sampling from stationary states, or fixed points, of bosonic Lindbladian dynamics with bounded-degree polynomial interactions. While the complexity of transient bosonic dynamics has been investigated, understanding the computational power of bosonic fixed points requires addressing subtleties of infinite-dimensional systems, including the existence, uniqueness, and convergence of stationary states. We establish a broad complexity landscape spanning universal quantum computation, efficient classical simulation, sampling hardness, and undecidability. First, we show that universal quantum computation can be embedded into observable estimation at the unique fixed point of a bosonic Lindbladian with a Hamiltonian of degree at most twelve and only linear photon loss. Moreover, this fixed point can be prepared from vacuum in polynomial time. On the classical side, we identify Gaussian regimes with incoherent pumping that admit efficient photon-number sampling and establish stability of classical approximability under sufficiently weak non-Gaussian Kerr perturbations. Conversely, for Gaussian fixed points without incoherent pumping, we establish hardness of exact sampling under constant-rate linear loss and hardness of approximate sampling at inverse-polynomial loss rates under standard boson-sampling conjectures. We also relate sampling from non-Gaussian fixed points to variants of boson sampling. Finally, we prove that deciding the existence of a stationary density operator is $\mathsf{RE}$-hard, even for purely dissipative Lindbladians with degree-five jump operators acting on at most four modes.

papers.title: Running-Time Lower Bounds under FPT $\neq$ W[1]
papers.abstract: We revisit running-time lower bounds historically based on the Exponential Time Hypothesis. Our case study asks how much of their quantitative content can be recovered under the assumption FPT $\neq$ W[1]. The reductions encode the choice of a clique in few bits and control the target parameter in terms of that encoding. This makes a sufficiently fast algorithm for the target problem yield a fixed-parameter algorithm for deciding whether a graph has a clique of the requested size. We obtain twelve lower bounds for deterministic algorithms across graph, string, and integer feasibility problems, including bounds that hold under structural restrictions. In several cases the same function of the parameter appears in the exponent as in the historical bound, with the additional requirement that the cutoff for any prescribed saving in the exponent be computable.

papers.title: Exponential Lower Bounds for 2-query Relaxed Locally Decodable Codes
authors: Alexander R. Block (University of Illinois at Chicago)
papers.abstract: Locally Decodable Codes (LDCs) are error-correcting codes $C\colon\Sigma^n\rightarrow \Sigma^m,$ encoding \emph{messages} in $\Sigma^n$ to \emph{codewords} in $\Sigma^m$, with super-fast decoding algorithms. They are important mathematical objects in many areas of theoretical computer science, yet the best constructions so far have codeword length $m$ that is super-polynomial in $n$, for codes with constant query complexity and constant alphabet size, while tolerating a constant-fraction of errors. In a very surprising result, Ben-Sasson, Goldreich, Harsha, Sudan, and Vadhan (SICOMP 2006) show how to construct a relaxed version of LDCs (RLDCs) with constant query complexity and slightly super-linear codeword length over the binary alphabet, and used them to obtain significantly-improved constructions of Probabilistically Checkable Proofs. In this work, we prove an exponential lower bound on the length of Hamming RLDCs making $2$ queries (even adaptively) over the binary alphabet. This answers a question explicitly raised by Gur and Lachish (SICOMP 2021) and is the first exponential lower bound for RLDCs. Combined with the results of Ben-Sasson et al., our result exhibits a "phase-transition"-type behavior on the codeword length for some constant-query complexity. We achieve these lower bounds via a transformation of RLDCs to LDCs, using a careful analysis of restrictions of message bits that fix codeword bits.

papers.title: A Non-Nested Quantum Search for TSP: Explicit Oracle Construction Beyond the $2^n$ Barrier
papers.abstract: The traveling salesman problem (TSP) is a classic NP-hard problem. Held--Karp dynamic programming~\cite{held1962dynamic, bellman1962dynamic} solves it exactly in $O(n^2 2^n)$ time. Ambainis et al.~\cite{ambainis2019quantum}\ (SODA~2019) proposed a hybrid classical-quantum dynamic programming that improved the query complexity to $O^*(1.727^n)$. However, their algorithm uses nested quantum minimum finding, which complicates coherent circuit implementation, particularly the handling of threshold updates within nested subroutines. To address this difficulty, we design a quantum divide-and-conquer framework without any recursive process. We overcome the oracle-construction bottleneck by preparing a set partition state, requiring $O(n^2)$ gates and $O(n)$ depth. Under assumed QRAM model, the structured state preparation enables polynomial-depth oracle evaluation, yielding an overall running time of $O^*(1.866^n)$ for TSP. Qiskit simulations for $n=6$ and 7, using QFT-based data loading in place of QRAM, yield empirical optimal-solution probabilities of $98.9\%$ and $100\%$, respectively, in fixed-threshold amplitude-amplification tests.

papers.title: Improved Separations between Quantum and Classical Communication Complexity of Total Functions
papers.abstract: We refine Gavinsky's framework (arXiv:2608.18784) for exponential separations between quantum and randomized communication complexity of total functions and obtain larger separations: polylogarithmic quantum communication versus $\tilde\Omega(\sqrt n)$ randomized communication with two quantum messages, and versus $\Omega(n^{1-\varepsilon})$ for every fixed $0<\varepsilon<1$ with more quantum messages. Our main technical contribution is a general conversion from quantum versus randomized communication separations for partial functions to separations for total functions. Our construction combines the communication lookup construction of Anshu, Belovs, Ben-David, G\"o\"os, Jain, Kothari, Lee, and Santha (FOCS 2016), the fully linear PCPs of Boneh, Boyle, Corrigan-Gibbs, Gilboa, and Ishai (CRYPTO 2019), and a linear seeded extractor with a short seed based on the construction of Raz, Reingold, and Vadhan (JCSS 2002). The key idea is to use the extractor to compress the lookup table into a single cell, thereby reducing the input length.

papers.title: When Matchgate Base Collapse Fails
papers.abstract: Base collapse in holographic algorithms asks whether the number of Boolean variables per edge can be bounded by the domain size alone. Chen (STOC 2016) and Xia (STOC 2016) proved collapse under full-rank and other structural hypotheses. We give a negative answer when several locally rank-deficient signatures share one encoding. For every $k\ge2$, we construct a four-label three-state language of maximum arity $k+2$, with $O(k)$-bit integer entries and minimum width $\Theta(2^{k/2}/k)$. The lower bound holds under exact labelled equivalence: competing presentations may change the domain and complex weights but must preserve every instance value on the same labelled planar graph. The lower bound follows from a dimension-counting argument in algebraic geometry: low-width representations force nontrivial polynomial relations among instance values. The matching upper bound uses determinant and Pfaffian interpolation. We also prove a trichotomy of column spaces for three-state presentations whose base has rank three and whose left matrix forms have column spaces spanning the dual domain space. One case has width at most three; each of the other two contains unbounded-width families.

papers.title: Sharp Bounds for Selector Advice and Oblivious Equilibrium Search
papers.abstract: Ko's tournament argument recognizes a P-selective language with quadratic advice. We determine the leading coefficient in the selector-query model. On $n$-bit inputs, $n^2/4+O(n)$ ordinary advice bits and $n$ nonadaptive comparisons suffice. Some cuts require $n^2/4-O(n\log n)$ bits even for randomized decoders with adaptive access to individual-degree-two extensions. At degree one the exact fixed advice width is $n+1$. Assuming exponential hardness in $\mathrm E$ against SAT-gate circuits, the quarter bound holds in deterministic polynomial time for every P-selective language. The same fixed point determines the cost of searching for an approximate equilibrium before seeing the payoffs. In an $N$-action symmetric constant-sum game with payoffs in $[0,1]$, let $P$ be the best worst-case probability that one game-independent proposal is an additive $\epsilon$-Nash equilibrium. For each fixed $0<\epsilon<1/2$, \[ -\log_2 P=(1+o(1))\, \frac{(\log_2 N)^2}{4[1-H_2(1/2+\epsilon)]}. \] The algorithm draws uniform actions and proposes their empirical distribution for both players. The lower bound allows arbitrary mixed profiles and $N^{o(1)}$ adaptive payoff inspections before the proposal. For all symmetric two-player games, including general-sum games, the sharp exponent is $(\ln 2/8+o(1))(\log_2 N)^2/\epsilon^2$ when $\epsilon\to0$ and $\log(1/\epsilon)=o(\log N)$. For security strategies in arbitrary zero-sum games the exponent is four times larger, and sampling an optimal strategy attains it. The common mechanism counts successful tuples. A fixed point makes them capture constant sampling probability while controlling a power moment of their distribution.
